report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Curriculum learning, the deliberate ordering of learning experiences, is central to how humans and animals learn, yet its benefits in neural networks are inconsistent.
We argue that curricula succeed when they prevent or correct early commitments that might otherwise predispose learners to underfit or overfit to training data.
Early experience can lead learners to overlook relevant information, or to rely on irrelevant details that do not generalise well.
Curricula help by preventing these mistakes or making them easier to correct.
Their benefits Glossary Anti-curriculum: training ordered from hard to easy.
Commitment: the tendency for early learning to establish particular features or patterns that continue to dominate later decisions.
Compression: concentrating a representation into fewer independent dimensions, potentially losing distinctions that the task requires.
Curriculum: any deliberate ordering of training experience, for example from simple to complex, easy to hard or proximal to distal.
Related schedules include blocking versus interleaving, pacing, and schedules over the information a learner can use.
Curricula differ from spacing schedules, which concern when material is revisited rather than the order in which its difficulty unfolds.
Effective capacity (effective degrees of freedom): how much task-relevant information a learner can actually represent and use, given its architecture, prior learning and training time.
Distinct from raw parameter or neurone count.
Effective rank and participation ratio: continuous counts of how many directions carry meaningful weight or variance in a representation.
Lazy and rich learning: in lazy learning, internal features barely change and learning is confined largely to the readout; in rich learning, internal features reorganise to fit the task.
Lottery ticket: in a large network, a sub-network that happens to be well initialised for the task.
Overfitting: learning a solution more complex than the task requires, which fits the training examples but generalises poorly.
Overparameterised: having many more parameters than a task strictly requires.
Pacing: how quickly the pool of training examples grows over time, independent of their order.
Readout: the final stage of a network, which maps its internal representation onto a decision.
In the brain, the neurones whose activity drives the response.
Readout subspace: the set of units or features that most strongly drive the learner's decision.
Task-appropriate dimensionality: representing enough independent dimensions to capture the distinctions the task requires, without relying on unnecessary ones.

Curricula diminish when learners have spare capacity or suitable representations, and curricula can even harm learning when early experience establishes patterns that later experience cannot build on.
The main source of curriculum benefit, thus, is helping learners 'unlearn' overly simple or overly complex solutions.
• Curricula are central to how humans and animals learn, yet in artificial neural networks their benefits are inconsistent and often vanish in large models.

• New work in humans and neural networks shows that easy-to-hard curricula help learners recover stimulus dimensions that earlier learning compressed away, and help most when there is more to recover.
• In perceptual learning, easy-first training instead leads learners to rely on fewer dimensions, which transfer better, so curricula can push representations towards fewer dimensions or more.
• Analytical theory shows that curriculum benefits shrink as networks widen or as regularisation takes over their role, and in language-model pretraining they fade with scale.
Curricula are central to human and animal learning Curriculum learning (CL; see Glossary) -the deliberate ordering of learning experiencesis foundational to how humans learn.
Developmental psychologists and educational theorists broadly agree that learners acquire knowledge progressively.
They build complex skills and ideas by mastering simpler problems first [1, 2], and benefit from revisiting familiar concepts at increasing levels of difficulty [3].
text.formatted: They build complex skills and ideas by mastering simpler problems first <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>, and benefit from revisiting familiar concepts at increasing levels of difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: One reason is that learning in smaller steps helps manage the amount of information a learner must process at once [4].
text.formatted: One reason is that learning in smaller steps helps manage the amount of information a learner must process at once <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Animal trainers also teach complex behaviours in small steps, a method known as shaping [5, 6].
text.formatted: Animal trainers also teach complex behaviours in small steps, a method known as shaping <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: Mathematical models show that shaping can be necessary when a task must be built from simpler parts [7].
text.formatted: Mathematical models show that shaping can be necessary when a task must be built from simpler parts <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Empirical studies across species and domains -from auditory identification in humans and rats [8], visual perceptual learning [9, 10], perceptual decision-making [11] and compositional generalisation [12, 13] -show that the structure of a training sequence can change both how quickly a skill is acquired and how far it transfers.
text.formatted: Empirical studies across species and domains -from auditory identification in humans and rats <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, visual perceptual learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>, perceptual decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> and compositional generalisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref> -show that the structure of a training sequence can change both how quickly a skill is acquired and how far it transfers.

text.text: But curricula do not always help.

Practice methods that help people learn simple motor skills do not always help with complex ones [14], and in human category learning, fading from easy to hard helped only when the relevant dimension had to be found among irrelevant ones [15] -that is, only when there was a risk of focusing on the wrong features.
text.formatted: Practice methods that help people learn simple motor skills do not always help with complex ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, and in human category learning, fading from easy to hard helped only when the relevant dimension had to be found among irrelevant ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> -that is, only when there was a risk of focusing on the wrong features.

text.text: Curricula are therefore well grounded in psychology, but their benefits depend on the learner and the task.
Human studies also show that what learners bring to a task matters.
People can combine familiar rules in new ways, a form of generalisation that standard neural networks often struggle with [12].
text.formatted: People can combine familiar rules in new ways, a form of generalisation that standard neural networks often struggle with <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: They benefit from training in which examples vary one feature at a time and are grouped into blocks [12, 16].
text.formatted: They benefit from training in which examples vary one feature at a time and are grouped into blocks <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: Networks can reproduce this pattern when learning is controlled by context [12, 13], although an alternative explanation is that learners rely more heavily on recent experience [17].
text.formatted: Networks can reproduce this pattern when learning is controlled by context <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>, although an alternative explanation is that learners rely more heavily on recent experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Either way, curricula interact with, rather than override, the learner's existing representational biases.
Neurophysiological studies show that learning in small steps can matter because of limits in the brain itself.
Monkeys learning to control a brain-computer interface could quickly master tasks that reused familiar patterns of neural activity, but struggled when success required entirely new patterns [18].
text.formatted: Monkeys learning to control a brain-computer interface could quickly master tasks that reused familiar patterns of neural activity, but struggled when success required entirely new patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that, despite having many neurones, the brain may initially be limited to a much smaller set of activity patterns it can readily produce, known as its intrinsic manifold.
However, this constraint is not absolute.

Monkeys could learn these harder tasks over several days, producing genuinely new activity patterns, but learning was supported by an incremental training procedure that progressively increased the demand, and was inconsistent without it [19].
text.formatted: Monkeys could learn these harder tasks over several days, producing genuinely new activity patterns, but learning was supported by an incremental training procedure that progressively increased the demand, and was inconsistent without it <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: This is the clearest neural case of a curriculum creating new directions for learning. help when they move learners towards it, from either side.
Underfitting: learning a solution too simple to capture the structure the task requires.
Unlearning: reopening or reshaping the representational directions that currently dominate behaviour -recovering dimensions compressed away, or releasing directions the task cannot use.
This is not forgetting, and is distinct from 'machine unlearning', the removal of specific training data from a trained model.
Curricula can make unlearning unnecessary (by shaping what is committed) or possible (by helping a committed learner recover what was compressed).
Weight decay: a common training penalty that keeps a network's weights small, discouraging reliance on many features.
XOR rule: a category rule in which the answer depends on a combination of two features, so neither feature alone predicts it.
In machine learning, the same principle is applied by deliberately sequencing training examples, often from easier to harder ones.
The concept was introduced to deep learning by Bengio et al. [20], who showed that training order can improve generalisation in neural networks.
text.formatted: The concept was introduced to deep learning by Bengio et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, who showed that training order can improve generalisation in neural networks.

text.text: Curricula have since improved transfer in visual learning [10, 21], stabilised early phases of language model pretraining [22, 23] and helped on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning [24, 25].

text.text: But there are also many cases in which curricula make no difference.

In standard supervised training with sufficient compute, curricula often perform comparably to random ordering [26]; in transformers, exhaustive evaluations conclude that data-based curricula rarely help [27]; and in post-training of language models for compositional reasoning, difficulty-ordered schedules show no reliable advantage over random sampling [28].

text.text: Some apparent successes and failures also reflect design choices rather than learning (Box 1).
So it remains unclear why curricula help in some cases but not others.
This article asks what properties of a learner determine whether curricula promote learning.
We propose that the benefit of a curriculum depends on how readily a learner can change what it has already learned.
Some learners have enough spare capacity to accommodate new information without disturbing existing representations.
Others must reorganise what they already know, which can be difficult once early learning has established a particular way of solving the task.
Building on recent work [29], we call this reorganisation 'unlearning'.
text.formatted: Building on recent work <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>, we call this reorganisation 'unlearning'.

text.text: Unlearning here does not mean forgetting, nor what AI researchers call 'machine unlearning', the removal of specific training data from a trained model [30].
text.formatted: Unlearning here does not mean forgetting, nor what AI researchers call 'machine unlearning', the removal of specific training data from a trained model <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: It means reopening or reshaping the dominant representational directions that currently govern task behaviour.
By a representational direction, we mean a feature or combination of features that a learner can use to make a distinction, such as colour or shape when learning to categorise objects.
Table 1 summarises the evidence reviewed below.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> summarises the evidence reviewed below.

text.text: In a recent study, curricula helped learners recover information they had previously overlooked [29]; in another study, curricula helped learners avoid relying on unnecessary information [10].
text.formatted: In a recent study, curricula helped learners recover information they had previously overlooked <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>; in another study, curricula helped learners avoid relying on unnecessary information <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Although these effects might seem to be in tension, we argue that both reflect the same principle -curricula are useful when they guide learning towards the representations a task actually requires.
Curricula can help learning via at least three routes.

They can provide useful feedback earlier (bridging time), make learning signals more reliable (aligning gradients), or guide learners towards the features needed for the task (finding the right directions).
We briefly cover the first two before turning to the third, which is the focus of this article.
In reinforcement learning, reward often arrives only at the end of a long sequence of actions, and a learner that rarely reaches the goal receives almost no signal to learn from.
Curricula bridge this gap.

Training a robot from start positions increasingly far from the goal gives it feedback from the start of training [31], and automated curricula that choose tasks the learner can only just solve work in the same way [32, 33].
text.formatted: Training a robot from start positions increasingly far from the goal gives it feedback from the start of training <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>, and automated curricula that choose tasks the learner can only just solve work in the same way <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33]</ref>.

text.text: The same gap arises when recurrent networks must hold information over time, and they learn memory tasks far more easily when the task is built up gradually [5, 34].

text.text: A second route concerns the direction of each learning step.
Hard or noisy examples can push a learner in unhelpful directions, whereas easy examples give cleaner signals.

Weinshall and colleagues proved that, for a linear model trained by gradient descent, learning converges faster on easier examples [37], suggesting that easy examples produce updates that point more directly towards the solution.

text.text: Under limited training budgets or with label noise, however, easy-to-hard curricula outperformed standard training.
In simple settings with a single best solution, such curricula make learning faster but do not improve the final result [40].
text.formatted: In simple settings with a single best solution, such curricula make learning faster but do not improve the final result <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: To change where learning ends up, and not just how fast it gets there, a curriculum must change which directions a network commits to.
Mannelli et al. [41] give the clearest mathematical account of how curricula help a network find the right directions, and we develop it further here.
text.formatted: Mannelli et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> give the clearest mathematical account of how curricula help a network find the right directions, and we develop it further here.

text.text: They use a small network learning a classification task that requires combining two features, rather than relying on either one alone.
The smallest network capable of solving the task has only four hidden units, each of which must learn to distinguish a different group of stimuli.
If these units initially learn the wrong distinctions, the network can become trapped in a poor solution.
An easy-first curriculum makes this less likely.
A larger network is less vulnerable because it has more units available, increasing the chance that some are already well placed to learn the task (a 'lottery ticket') [49].
text.formatted: A larger network is less vulnerable because it has more units available, increasing the chance that some are already well placed to learn the task (a 'lottery ticket') <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref>.

text.text: With these spare resources, the order of training matters less.
A learner with spare capacity can absorb new demands in unused directions without reorganising existing ones, and so has nothing to unlearn.
This might seem to imply that humans, with billions of neurones, should rarely need curricula.

But capacity is relative to the task and the time available, and on short timescales people attend to only a few dimensions at once [4, 29] and can readily produce only a small set of neural activity patterns [18], so their effective capacity for a new task is often small.

text.text: Constrained learners, biological and artificial, behave like the small network.
Strittmatter et al. [11] trained a parsimonious two-layer network and human participants on an equivalent XOR-like decision task.
text.formatted: Strittmatter et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> trained a parsimonious two-layer network and human participants on an equivalent XOR-like decision task.

text.text: In both, an ascending (easy-to-hard) curriculum produced the best test performance and a 'bad' blocked sequence impaired it.

In networks the damage persisted through extended training, because the network had committed to a sub-task solution from which its few units could not escape, whereas networks trained on hard or random sequences eventually caught up.
Whether the human impairment lasts was not tested.
For a learner with little spare capacity, what it learns first matters more than how much it sees.
This also explains why curricula so often fail in large models, which usually have little to unlearn.
In heavily overparameterised networks, suitable directions are likely to exist already [41].
text.formatted: In heavily overparameterised networks, suitable directions are likely to exist already <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: A related explanation may apply when fine-tuning pretrained models.
Rather than learning everything from scratch, these models can often adapt to new tasks through relatively small changes to what they already know.
Indeed, many fine-tuning objectives can be optimised by adjusting only a small number of directions in parameter space [46].
text.formatted: Indeed, many fine-tuning objectives can be optimised by adjusting only a small number of directions in parameter space <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>.

text.text: The key idea is that capacity must be judged relative to what the learner is trying to achieve, and how much training time it has.
Even a very large model may be effectively constrained when it must learn from an enormous dataset in a limited number of steps.
Modern pretraining usually passes through its vast dataset only once, so the order of the earliest training, while representations are still forming, matters most.
Within pretraining, the effect fades with scale [42].
text.formatted: Within pretraining, the effect fades with scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, the full training pipeline of modern language models is itself a curriculum.

A later 'mid-training' stage shifts training towards higher-quality data [50], and reinforcement learning in post-training helps mainly when the pretrained model already shows some ability on the task [28], as a model that never succeeds has no reward to learn from.
text.formatted: A later 'mid-training' stage shifts training towards higher-quality data <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>, and reinforcement learning in post-training helps mainly when the pretrained model already shows some ability on the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>, as a model that never succeeds has no reward to learn from.

text.text: Choices about design, controls and evaluation can determine whether a curriculum appears to succeed.
Six common problems can create or hide curriculum effects.
A curriculum can change both the order in which examples appear and how quickly new examples are introduced.
These are different interventions -a learner might benefit simply because it sees a gradually expanding training set, rather than because easier examples come first [26, 51].
text.formatted: These are different interventions -a learner might benefit simply because it sees a gradually expanding training set, rather than because easier examples come first <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51]</ref>.

text.text: Wu et al.'s 'random curriculum', which expands the training set in random order, performed comparably to the best curricula under standard conditions, so many reported curriculum gains are pacing gains -implicit regularisation through a growing dataset -rather than ordering gains.
Some studies labelled as curriculum learning test pacing alone.

The document-understanding 'curriculum' of Hamdan et al. [52], for instance, expands the data in stages without ordering by difficulty, and its benefit appeared for a text-only language model but not for one that also sees page layout.
text.formatted: The document-understanding 'curriculum' of Hamdan et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref>, for instance, expands the data in stages without ordering by difficulty, and its benefit appeared for a text-only language model but not for one that also sees page layout.

text.text: The cleanest control presents exactly the same examples, with the same difficulty distribution, in shuffled order [41, 42].

text.text: A related confound is recency.
A curriculum that ends on the hardest material may look better at test simply because its final block most resembles the test.

Appending an identical balanced block to every condition before testing controls for this, and in Rubruck et al.'s networks the curriculum benefit for exceptions remained after this control, whereas the cost of the reverse curriculum disappeared [29].
text.formatted: Appending an identical balanced block to every condition before testing controls for this, and in Rubruck et al.'s networks the curriculum benefit for exceptions remained after this control, whereas the cost of the reverse curriculum disappeared <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: An example that is difficult for one model may be straightforward for another, so common measures of difficulty, such as example length or prediction error, do not reliably identify which examples should come first [27].

text.text: And proxies for difficulty carry other variables with them, so that sorting a pretraining corpus by linguistic difficulty also reorders its source domains [42].

text.text: It is not that difficulty is undefinable, but rather that it depends on the model, the objective and the training conditions.
If one training schedule uses more computation than another, its apparent advantage may have little to do with the curriculum itself.

Studies should therefore match training examples, steps or total computation, not just epochs, because computation can differ even at a matched number of steps when example length tracks difficulty [28].

text.text: The learning rate.
A curriculum's effect depends on how the learning rate changes during training.

In solvable models, the optimal joint schedule drops the learning rate sharply at the easy-to-hard transition, and with a properly adjusted learning rate an easy-tohard curriculum becomes optimal where it otherwise was not [56].
text.formatted: In solvable models, the optimal joint schedule drops the learning rate sharply at the easy-to-hard transition, and with a properly adjusted learning rate an easy-tohard curriculum becomes optimal where it otherwise was not <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref>.

text.text: Comparisons should either hold the learning-rate schedule fixed across conditions or optimise it separately for each, and say which.
The choice of test.
A curriculum may leave overall accuracy unchanged while improving how well learners handle unfamiliar examples or exceptions to a rule.

Volk et al.'s key outcome is transfer to new conditions [10], Curriculum by Smoothing reports transfer and domain-adaptation gains [21], and Maharana and Bansal [24] found curriculum benefits for out-of-distribution generalisation but not for in-distribution accuracy.

text.text: Studies evaluating only aggregate in-distribution metrics may miss representational effects entirely.
Time course.
Readout subspaces can stabilise within ∼200 steps [10], Wu et al. [26] find effects under time constraints, and Zhang et al. [23] report gains in early and mid-training.

text.text: At the other extreme, some effects appear only late.
In small language models, the stability benefits of curricula became apparent only as training approached 300 billion tokens, and were invisible at 10-60 billion [42].
text.formatted: In small language models, the stability benefits of curricula became apparent only as training approached 300 billion tokens, and were invisible at 10-60 billion <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: Studies that look only at final performance, or at a single point in training, can miss how a curriculum works.
Tracking how a learner's representations change during training, for example their dimensionality along task-relevant axes, can show what the curriculum is doing [57].
text.formatted: Tracking how a learner's representations change during training, for example their dimensionality along task-relevant axes, can show what the curriculum is doing <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should therefore include pacing and matched-exposure controls, control for recency at test, enforce compute parity, hold or co-optimise learning-rate schedules, report learning dynamics over both early and late training, and evaluate transfer, out-ofdistribution or item-specific outcomes.

(A) On a simple task, unguided learning may follow such features, forming spurious channels that reach no plants.
This is overfitting.
(B) On a complex task, it may instead settle into too few channels, leaving some plants dry.
This is underfitting.
These are possible failures of unguided learning rather than inevitable ones, and which arises depends on the demands of the task relative to the learner's capacity.
(C) Guiding the first flow towards useful directions prevents spurious channels, so unlearning is unnecessary.
(D) Opening new channels gradually from an established one lets neglected directions be recovered, making unlearning possible.
Curricula help most when early channels would otherwise be hard to change.
They matter less when a learner has spare capacity or already has suitable channels, and they can make matters worse when the first channels lead the wrong way.

This can go wrong in two ways.
If the water settles into just one channel, some plants are left dry.
If it follows every small, temporary dip in the ground, it is wasted on channels that reach no plants.
Once channels are deep, redirecting the water is difficult, especially when there is little room to form new ones.
A gardener can help by guiding the first flow towards the main plants, then gradually opening new channels as needed, but guiding it the wrong way makes matters worse.
Learning works much the same way.
In our analogy, plants are the task, water is experience, and the channels represent directions in the internal representations of a neural network.
Early learning commits a learner to a small set of these directions, often within the first few hundred training steps [10].

text.text: Alternatively, it can overfit by relying on details that happen to predict the training examples but do not hold for new ones [10, 56].

text.text: Fixing underfitting means recovering a dimension that was compressed away, and fixing overfitting means letting go of an unhelpful one.
Curricula, the gardener in this picture, can help with both, to the extent that they move a learner towards task-appropriate dimensionality (Box 2).
Early commitments matter because they are hard to reverse.

Early training is a critical period in deep networks -deficits imposed at the start can permanently impair what a network learns [59], and networks that continue from earlier training generalise worse than those trained from scratch [60].
text.formatted: Early training is a critical period in deep networks -deficits imposed at the start can permanently impair what a network learns <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref>, and networks that continue from earlier training generalise worse than those trained from scratch <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>.

text.text: Restoring lost plasticity requires explicit interventions such as reinitialising little-used units [61].
text.formatted: Restoring lost plasticity requires explicit interventions such as reinitialising little-used units <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref>.

text.text: Compression is especially hard to undo.
Networks trained from small initial weights tend to learn the strongest patterns first [58].
text.formatted: Networks trained from small initial weights tend to learn the strongest patterns first <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref>.

text.text: Once a relevant feature has been neglected, it contributes little to the network's responses, leaving little learning signal to reveal its importance [29].
text.formatted: Once a relevant feature has been neglected, it contributes little to the network's responses, leaving little learning signal to reveal its importance <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Humans show a similar difficulty.
Having learned that a stimulus dimension is irrelevant, people can perform hundreds of trials without noticing that it has become fully predictive [62].
text.formatted: Having learned that a stimulus dimension is irrelevant, people can perform hundreds of trials without noticing that it has become fully predictive <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[62]</ref>.

text.text: Three things need to be distinguished -what a learner could represent (its model capacity), what it currently represents (its representational dimensionality), and how easily those representations can change.
A network may have many parameters but use only a few representational dimensions when solving a particular task.
Conversely, a smaller network may already use most of the resources available to it.
Our account predicts that curriculum benefits depend on this difference between available and already-used capacity, and on whether the learner's existing features are useful for the task.
Effective capacity should be assessed before, or independently of, training on the curriculum.

Width relative to the minimal sufficient architecture, initialisation scale, training time and the rank of the readout all contribute, and so does prior knowledge, since a learner whose features are already aligned with the task needs to recruit little.
In small networks, capacity can be indexed by width relative to the minimal architecture that can solve the task -four hidden units for the XOR-like Gaussian mixture [41] -and by the training budget.

text.text: A second axis is how freely internal features can change.

Networks initialised at large scale learn 'lazily', using their existing features differently while barely changing them, whereas small-scale initialisation produces 'rich' learning, in which the network changes its internal representations as it trains [63].
text.formatted: Networks initialised at large scale learn 'lazily', using their existing features differently while barely changing them, whereas small-scale initialisation produces 'rich' learning, in which the network changes its internal representations as it trains <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref>.

text.text: The degree of richness can be estimated from how task-relevant representational manifolds become separable during learning [57], and rich dynamics tend to learn easy examples before hard ones even without a curriculum [64].
text.formatted: The degree of richness can be estimated from how task-relevant representational manifolds become separable during learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref>, and rich dynamics tend to learn easy examples before hard ones even without a curriculum <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[64]</ref>.

text.text: Having a large set of fixed features does not necessarily make a learner insensitive to training order.
Even if the features themselves barely change, early experience can determine which ones the learner comes to rely on.

In Volk et al.'s perceptual-learning model, readout weights changed about 200 times more than those of earlier layers, and freezing the sensory network left behaviour and generalisation unchanged, yet with short training and few samples, which readout directions were selected still depended on the training trajectory [10].

text.text: Dimensionality relative to the task can be summarised by the participation ratio or effective rank of a representation -a continuous count of how many dimensions carry meaningful variance [65] -but total dimensionality is ambiguous, because a curriculum may need to raise it (to recover a compressed dimension) or lower it (to release an unhelpful one).

text.text: It is better measured separately along task-defined axes.
Rubruck et al.
projected hidden representations onto a rule axis and an exception axis, and found that the curriculum expanded the exception axis while leaving the rule axis unchanged [29].

text.text: The direction of change differs across settings.

In perceptual learning, curricula lowered readout rank [10]; in category learning, they raised representational dimensionality [29]; and in small language models, whose output layer is too low-rank to represent the distribution over words (the 'softmax bottleneck') [43], random data ordering drove the output layer's singular-value spectrum to become sharply concentrated late in training, and curricula prevented this [42].

text.text: The measure that predicts benefit, and the expected direction of change, must therefore be specified in advance from the task's structure.
Unlearning in humans cannot yet be measured directly, but there are behavioural and neural proxies.

Reaction-time costs for exception items, and slowing when a given stimulus feature changes between trials, index which dimensions a participant is attending to [29]; and representations in ventromedial prefrontal cortex compress during concept learning [66].

text.text: Extending Mannelli et al.'s analysis [41], our proposal is that curricula help learners avoid or overcome early commitments that would otherwise be difficult to change.
text.formatted: Extending Mannelli et al.'s analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>, our proposal is that curricula help learners avoid or overcome early commitments that would otherwise be difficult to change.

text.text: They can do this in two ways.
First, a curriculum can guide early learning towards the features that matter, preventing the learner from relying on irrelevant ones, which makes unlearning unnecessary.

Second, when earlier learning has caused important information to be overlooked, a curriculum can introduce new demands gradually enough for that information to be recovered, which makes unlearning possible.
In the garden analogy, the first approach prevents water from entering unnecessary channels, while the second helps it reach plants that were initially left dry.
Curricula should therefore help most when learners have limited capacity or training time, and when their initial commitments are difficult to reverse.
When learners can easily accommodate new information, the order of training matters less.
A curriculum's value, in short, is the unlearning it saves.
A mathematical analysis supports this account.

Using a simplified network model that can be solved exactly, Mignacco and Mori [56] show that good generalisation requires aligning weights with the task-relevant directions while keeping weight on irrelevant directions small.
text.formatted: Using a simplified network model that can be solved exactly, Mignacco and Mori <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref> show that good generalisation requires aligning weights with the task-relevant directions while keeping weight on irrelevant directions small.

text.text: Easy-tohard curricula mainly serve the second goal, suppressing growth along irrelevant directions early.
Interestingly, this benefit disappears when the network is already discouraged from relying on unnecessary features through weight decay, a common form of regularisation.
Under these conditions, the best schedule instead runs from hard to easy.
A curriculum is therefore only one way to keep the wrong features from dominating learning, and when another mechanism already does this, a curriculum may have little to add.
However, the absence of anything to unlearn is not the only cause of failure.
Curricula also fail, and can actively harm, when what is learned from the easy examples cannot be built on for the hard ones.
Controlled studies show this clearly.

In Strittmatter et al.'s study [11], a badly ordered sequence of blocks trapped the network, and in Mannelli et al.'s analysis [41], starting with very easy, low-noise examples committed the network to the nearest poor solution.

text.text: How transitions between difficulty levels are managed also matters.
Learners with limited capacity may struggle when task demands change abruptly.
Gradual transitions allow them to build on what they have already learned, rather than having to abandon it and start again.
In a theoretical model, the benefit of a curriculum also depends on preserving what was learned before moving to the next difficulty level [40].
text.formatted: In a theoretical model, the benefit of a curriculum also depends on preserving what was learned before moving to the next difficulty level <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: Human learning research offers a further counterpoint.
Interleaving examples of different categories, rather than blocking them, often improves category induction [67].
text.formatted: Interleaving examples of different categories, rather than blocking them, often improves category induction <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[67]</ref>.

text.text: This need not contradict the present account, since interleaving keeps every discriminating dimension in play and so guards against compression, but it cautions against equating a curriculum with blocked, easy-first ordering.
Two examples, underfitting and overfitting

The clearest evidence that curricula help learners unlearn comes from Rubruck and colleagues [29], who studied how humans and neural networks learn rules with exceptions, and who name the phenomenon 'curriculum unlearning'.
text.formatted: The clearest evidence that curricula help learners unlearn comes from Rubruck and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>, who studied how humans and neural networks learn rules with exceptions, and who name the phenomenon 'curriculum unlearning'.

text.text: Imagine learning to classify objects by colour, only to discover that a few exceptions also require you to consider their shape.
In their version of a classic task [68], six of eight stimuli could be classified using a single feature, but two required an additional distinction.
text.formatted: In their version of a classic task <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref>, six of eight stimuli could be classified using a single feature, but two required an additional distinction.

text.text: Both humans and networks initially learned the simpler rule and applied it even to the exceptions, classifying them below chance, which suggests that they had overlooked information needed for the full task.

Presenting rule stimuli first and introducing exceptions gradually increased the proportion of participants who reached the full rule-plus-exception strategy at test (65.3% against 44.4% without a curriculum), whereas the reverse order selectively harmed exception learning.
An earlier study using the same kind of task found that delaying exceptions also improved their learning, in humans and in a model of the hippocampus [69].
text.formatted: An earlier study using the same kind of task found that delaying exceptions also improved their learning, in humans and in a model of the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref>.

text.text: On our account, gradually introducing exceptions may have helped learners adapt the initial rule, rather than continuing to apply it indiscriminately.

In the networks, the curriculum raised the dimensionality of the hidden representation, specifically by separating the exceptions along a direction orthogonal to the rule, and final dimensionality predicted exception accuracy (𝑟 = 0.70).
A second experiment directly tested whether curricula help more when there is more to unlearn.
Networks first trained on a simple rule came to rely on almost a single dimension of information (participation ratio 1.09), whereas networks trained on a more complex rule retained several (2.93).
The curriculum benefit was roughly three times larger in the networks whose representations had been more strongly compressed.

The same interaction appeared in over a thousand human participants, and a reaction-time index of selective attention during pretraining -a behavioural proxy for compression -predicted who would later benefit from the curriculum.
When the networks' hidden layer was frozen, so that pretraining could not compress it, a curriculum benefit remained but no longer depended on pretraining.
As Rubruck et al. conclude, curricula on this evidence help more with unlearning than with learning from scratch -and the more there is to unlearn, the more they help.
Volk et al. [10] studied the opposite case, a simple task in which the risk is overfitting.
text.formatted: Volk et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> studied the opposite case, a simple task in which the risk is overfitting.

text.text: Human observers, and a network pretrained to recognise everyday images, learned to discriminate the orientation of visual patterns, with easy trials using large differences in orientation and hard trials small ones, and were then tested on new conditions.
Some learned easy trials before hard ones, while others saw only hard trials, or both kinds shuffled together.
In the network, nearly all learning took place in the readout, the final stage that turns features into a decision (Box 2).
Easy-first training led this decision-making layer to rely on fewer dimensions of information.
Importantly, networks that relied on fewer dimensions also performed better when tested on unfamiliar conditions (𝑟 = -0.69, and 𝑟 = -0.95 when the proportion of early easy trials was varied).

Transferring this simpler decision-making layer to a network trained only on hard examples also improved its generalisation, even beyond the sequential curriculum, suggesting that the way learning selects features is itself important.

Humans given shuffled easy and hard trials generalised, on average, as well as those given an explicit sequence, but with much greater variability, and observers who spontaneously learned easy trials first transferred best (𝑟 = 0.45).
Human learners, it seems, can partly supply their own curricula.
The following interpretation goes beyond Volk et al.'s framing.
Easy-first exposure prevents premature commitment to a high-dimensional, idiosyncratic readout.
Easy examples appear to help the learner identify the features that matter most.
Harder examples can then refine those distinctions, rather than encouraging the learner to rely on additional, less reliable features.
This is unlearning made unnecessary.
At first, these findings seem contradictory.
In one study, curricula helped learners focus on a smaller set of distinctions; in the other, they helped learners represent additional information.
But the difference makes sense once we consider what each task actually requires.
Rubruck et al.'s curriculum rescues a complex task from underfitting, whereas Volk et al.'s protects a simple task from overfitting.
Orientation discrimination needs only one key direction, and harder trials refine it, so the best solution is compact.
The rule-plus-exception task needs a second direction that the rule does not contain, so the best solution is larger than the learner's first guess.
In both cases, the curriculum helps learners establish what matters before harder examples shape their representations.
Sometimes this prevents unnecessary features from being learned; other times it allows previously neglected features to emerge.
The goal, then, is not always to represent fewer distinctions or more of them, but to represent the right ones for the task, which we call task-appropriate dimensionality.

Rubruck et al.'s frozen-network control suggests that the two ways in which curricula help can be dissociated, since the benefit that remained, like Volk et al.'s, lived in the readout and did not depend on prior compression.
Curriculum learning is often framed as a universal heuristic -teach easy before hard.
The evidence reviewed here supports a more precise and psychologically aligned conclusion.
Curricula are most valuable when learning is constrained and early experience risks establishing patterns that are difficult to change.
Under these conditions curricula succeed in one of two ways.
A curriculum can make unlearning unnecessary by helping learners identify the right features from the start.
Alternatively, it can make unlearning possible by gradually helping learners recover information they previously overlooked.
Either way, the target is task-appropriate dimensionality -a solution neither too simple nor too complex for the task -not low dimensionality as such.

Curricula fail in two complementary ways -when abundant capacity, aligned priors or regularisation render unlearning unnecessary, and when what is learned from easy examples cannot be built on for hard ones, making unlearning impossible.
The account makes falsifiable predictions (Box 3).
The account has several limitations.
It is best supported in small or analytically tractable learners, and the interaction between prior compression and capacity is predicted rather than shown.
Direct evidence that curricula help learners unlearn comes mainly from one category-learning paradigm [29] and from brain-computer interface learning in monkeys [19].

text.text: Not every curriculum effect is about unlearning either.
Bridging time and aligning gradients work differently, and the three routes should be distinguished experimentally (see Outstanding questions ).

The important question is therefore not simply whether curricula work, but what a learner has already learned, what prevents it from learning more, and whether its existing representations can accommodate new demands.
A theory of when curricula help is really a theory of what makes learning hard, and testing it means measuring capacity, compression, and interference in both brains and networks.
Box 3.
Predictions The account makes testable predictions.
For each, we state what result would show it to be wrong.
Dimensionality explains the benefit.
A curriculum should help when it changes which features a learner relies on, bringing them closer to those the task actually requires.

Curriculum benefit should be statistically mediated by an early shift towards task-appropriate dimensionality, measured along task-defined axes -contraction along unhelpful directions where the risk is over-commitment, expansion along compressed task-relevant directions where the risk is compression.
Equalising this shift across conditions, for example by transplanting a readout subspace as Volk et al. did [10], should abolish most of the curriculum benefit.
Rubruck et al.'s finding that final dimensionality predicts exception accuracy is consistent with this [29], but the stronger, causal test remains open.
The account is undermined if curricula improve performance without any shift in task-relative dimensionality.
Capacity gates unlearning.
The more strongly prior learning has restricted a learner's representations, the more it should benefit from a curriculum, especially when capacity is limited.
Rubruck et al.
showed that curriculum benefits scale with prior compression in small networks undergoing rich learning [29].

text.text: If effective capacity governs how much there is to unlearn, this interaction should be strongest in narrow, richly trained networks, weaker in wide ones -whose spare directions can absorb exceptions without recovering a compressed one -and absent when features cannot be compressed at all, as their frozen-network control already suggests.
In Mannelli et al.'s analysis, curriculum gains already peaked at intermediate noise levels and, in networks trained on noise-corrupted images, first rose and then fell as width increased [41].

text.text: The account is undermined if the compression-by-curriculum interaction is unaffected by width or by whether learning is lazy or rich.
Not all limits on learning should increase the value of a curriculum.
Reducing effective capacity without aligning it -fewer hidden units, a shorter training budget, a lower-rank readoutshould increase curriculum benefits in a model that normally shows none.

Constraining capacity in a task-aligned way -weight decay that suppresses irrelevant directions [56], a pre-selected readout subspace [10], or pretrained features matched to the task -should reduce or abolish them.

Bandwidth substitution.
If curricula work by controlling which information shapes early learning, restricting that information directly should produce some of the same benefits.
Curriculum by Smoothing already shows that a schedule on internal information flow can help.

It improved top-1 accuracy (for example, from 62.4% to 65.4% for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100), whereas smoothing the input images instead hurt, and holding the smoothing constant rather than annealing it fell below the unsmoothed baseline [21].

If curricula act by scheduling which directions are available for commitment, then gating the information available to internal features should reproduce part of the benefit of ordering even when the data are shuffled, and combining the two should yield sub-additive gains, because both act on the same early commitment.
A similar test could be run in transformers.
Scale and persistence in language models.
Larger language models should benefit less from curricula, but benefits established early in pretraining may persist even after training becomes randomly ordered.
Both patterns have already been reported at a fixed token budget [23, 42].

Non-monotonic alignment.
Curricula should help most when the easy and hard phases share some, but not all, of the same structure.

More precisely, the benefit should be negligible when the easy phase already contains the full solution, largest at intermediate overlap, and negative when what is learned in the easy phase cannot be built on in the hard phase.

Interference in continual learning likewise depends non-monotonically on task similarity [70], and task similarity determines whether networks learn new tasks lazily, with little forgetting, or richly, with substantial forgetting [71].

text.text: Human learners.
People should benefit most from explicit curricula when earlier learning has caused them to overlook important information.

Beyond category learning [29], this means that learners who arrive more compressed, and those who do not spontaneously learn easy material first when given shuffled practice [10], should benefit most.

• Do learners with stronger biases towards simple solutions benefit more from curricula on complex tasks, and less on simple ones?

Water flowing through a garden illustrates how early learning shapes what can be learned later.Channels stand for the directions a learner comes to rely on, plants for the demands of the task, and small dips for features that happen to predict the training examples.
Numbers show the order in which channels form, and lighter channels form later.
(A) On a simple task, unguided learning may follow such features, forming spurious channels that reach no plants.
This is overfitting.
(B) On a complex task, it may instead settle into too few channels, leaving some plants dry.
This is underfitting.
These are possible failures of unguided learning rather than inevitable ones, and which arises depends on the demands of the task relative to the learner's capacity.
(C) Guiding the first flow towards useful directions prevents spurious channels, so unlearning is unnecessary.
(D) Opening new channels gradually from an established one lets neglected directions be recovered, making unlearning possible.
Curricula help most when early channels would otherwise be hard to change.
They matter less when a learner has spare capacity or already has suitable channels, and they can make matters worse when the first channels lead the wrong way.
